summary: A socialist country in the eastern Indochinese Peninsula, long influenced by Chinese culture, which went through French colonization and the Vietnam War, and whose economy grew rapidly after the "Đổi Mới" (renovation) reforms of 1986.

ranking.name: No religion (including folk religion)
ranking.description: Vietnamese commonly keep an ancestral altar at home and honor ancestors on festivals and death anniversaries; they also worship folk deities such as the city god (Thành Hoàng) and the Mother Goddess (Đạo Mẫu), but these practices have no initiation ritual, so many people are classified as having no religion in surveys. After the communist regime was established in North Vietnam in 1945 and the country was reunified in 1975, the state promoted Marxist atheism and restricted the activities of religious organizations, which also led many people to stop registering a religion. In 2016 the "Practices related to the Viet beliefs in the Mother Goddesses of Three Realms" was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In the 17th century Portuguese and French missionaries came to Vietnam, and figures such as Alexandre de Rhodes built up solid Catholic communities. In the 19th century Nguyen-dynasty rulers such as Minh Mang persecuted Catholics, and France, using the protection of missionaries as a pretext, sent troops to Da Nang in 1858, beginning the process of colonizing Vietnam. When Vietnam was partitioned in 1954, several hundred thousand northern Catholics moved south, so Catholicism has important influence in the south; in 1988 the pope canonized 117 Vietnamese martyrs.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Mahayana Buddhism arrived around the 2nd century from India via China and by sea; the Ly dynasty (1009-1225) and the Tran dynasty strongly supported it, and in 1299 the retired emperor Tran Nhan Tong founded the Truc Lam Zen school. In 1963 the South Vietnamese Ngo Dinh Diem government suppressed Buddhism, and Thich Quang Duc set himself on fire in Saigon in protest, shocking the world. Because Buddhism is deeply blended with folk religion, the number of people actually taking part in temple activities is far greater than the registered Buddhist share.

ranking.name: Hoa Hao
ranking.description: Hoa Hao was founded in 1939 by Huynh Phu So in An Giang Province in the Mekong Delta; it is a reformist Buddhist movement that advocates lay practice and simplified ritual, and it quickly attracted large numbers of peasants. In the late French colonial period and during the Vietnam War, Hoa Hao organized its own armed forces, and after the war it was tightly controlled by the communist government. Its followers remain concentrated mainly in Mekong Delta provinces such as An Giang and Dong Thap.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: American Christian and Missionary Alliance missionaries began preaching in Da Nang in 1911, and Protestantism developed slowly during the French colonial period. Since the 1990s Protestantism has spread rapidly through radio evangelism among minority peoples such as the Ede and Jarai of the Central Highlands and the Hmong of the northern mountains, but the government, worried about its combination with political movements, has long restricted it, and the share of followers remains low.

religion.background: Vietnam's traditional religion is centered on ancestor worship, blending the "Three Teachings" of Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism with the worship of local deities in different places. Catholicism arrived in the 17th century, and the persecution of the Nguyen dynasty in the 19th century became one of the pretexts for the French invasion. In the 20th century, indigenous new religions such as Hoa Hao and Cao Dai appeared in the south. Under communist rule, from 1945 in the north and from 1975 across the whole country, the state promoted atheism and controlled religious organizations; after the "Đổi Mới" policy of 1986 religious activity was gradually relaxed, but it is still supervised by the state.

ranking.name: Vietnamese
ranking.description: Vietnamese belongs to the Austroasiatic family; Chinese rule over northern Vietnam for a thousand years, from 111 BCE to 938 CE, caused Vietnamese to absorb a large amount of Sino-Vietnamese vocabulary, and it was long written with Chinese characters and the self-created "chữ Nôm." In the 17th century Portuguese and French missionaries recorded Vietnamese in the Latin alphabet, and in 1651 de Rhodes published his Vietnamese-Portuguese-Latin dictionary, forming "chữ Quốc ngữ"; the French colonial authorities promoted Quốc ngữ, and in 1945 the Democratic Republic of Vietnam launched a literacy campaign that made it widespread. The Kinh make up nearly 90 percent of the population, so Vietnamese is the mother tongue of the great majority of citizens.

ranking.name: Hmong (Miao)
ranking.description: The Hmong (Miao) moved into the high mountain areas of northern Vietnam, such as around Ha Giang and Lao Cai, mainly from southern China in the 18th and 19th centuries, and live by upland farming. Hmong belongs to the Hmong-Mien family, and writing systems in the Latin alphabet appeared from the 1950s. Because they live in remote places and have little contact with the Kinh, the Hmong still mostly use their mother tongue, though the younger generation learns Vietnamese at school.

ranking.name: Khmer
ranking.description: Khmer is the language of the Khmer people (Khmer Krom) of provinces such as Soc Trang and Tra Vinh in the Mekong Delta. This land originally belonged to the Khmer Empire and was gradually brought into the territory by the Nguyen lords during Vietnam's "southward advance" of the 17th-18th centuries; the Khmer who remained there kept their own language and Theravada Buddhism, and the temples are still important places for teaching the Khmer script.

language.history: Vietnamese belongs to the Mon-Khmer branch of the Austroasiatic family and during a thousand years of Chinese rule absorbed a great deal of Chinese vocabulary; Chinese characters were the formal writing system for a long time, while chữ Nôm developed among the people. In the 17th century Western missionaries created the Latinized Quốc ngữ, in the early 20th century the French colonial government abolished the civil service examinations and promoted Quốc ngữ, and after 1945 Quốc ngữ became the only formal script. Vietnam has 54 officially recognized ethnic groups, and many minority languages such as Tày, Thai, Hmong and Khmer are still in use.

ranking.name: Phở
ranking.description: A clear broth simmered from beef or chicken bones with charred onion, ginger, star anise and cinnamon, in which rice noodles and slices of beef or chicken are served, accompanied by herbs, bean sprouts and lime.
ranking.history: Phở is generally believed to have been born in the early 20th century in the Hanoi and Nam Dinh area during the French colonial period: the French ate a lot of beef, which made materials such as beef bones easy to obtain, while the use of rice noodles and spices shows the influence of Chinese food. Explanations of the name's origin include derivation from the French "pot-au-feu" (beef stew) or the Cantonese "ngau yuk fan" (beef noodles). When Vietnam was partitioned in 1954, northern migrants brought phở to the south, and after 1975 Vietnamese refugees spread it around the world.

ranking.name: Bánh mì
ranking.description: A French baguette is filled with pâté, sliced pork or ham, pickled carrot and daikon, cucumber, cilantro and chili, with a crisp crust and a sour, sweet, salty and savory filling.
ranking.history: The baguette was brought to Vietnam by the French colonists in the late 19th century, and Vietnamese bakers added rice flour to make the bread lighter and crisper. After French influence withdrew in the 1950s, street vendors in Saigon began putting Vietnamese-flavored fillings in the bread, developing today's bánh mì. After 1975 Vietnamese refugees took it to the United States and elsewhere, and in 2011 the word "bánh mì" was added to the Oxford English Dictionary.

ranking.name: Gỏi cuốn (fresh spring rolls)
ranking.description: Moistened rice paper is wrapped around fresh shrimp, sliced pork, rice vermicelli, lettuce and herbs, rolled into a translucent cylinder and dipped in peanut sauce or a fish-sauce dip.
ranking.history: Fresh spring rolls are a representative snack of southern Vietnam; the rice paper used is a product of the rice culture of the Mekong Delta, and the abundant fresh herbs reflect the produce of the southern tropical climate. Unlike the deep-fried spring rolls of the north, fresh rolls are not cooked or fried, and have a refreshing texture. After 1975 Vietnamese emigrants brought them to the West, and they became one of the most popular appetizers in Vietnamese restaurants abroad.

ranking.name: Bún chả
ranking.description: Marinated sliced pork and pork patties are grilled over charcoal until fragrant and placed in a sweet and sour fish-sauce broth, to be dipped and eaten with rice vermicelli and plenty of lettuce and herbs.
ranking.history: Bún chả is a representative dish of the capital, Hanoi; Hanoians usually eat it at lunchtime, and the smoky aroma of charcoal grilling in the street is a typical scene of the Old Quarter. In 2016 U.S. President Obama and the celebrity chef Anthony Bourdain shared bún chả at a small restaurant in Hanoi, and the scene drew worldwide attention; the restaurant even boxed up and preserved the table they used. The dish has thus become a must-try for foreign visitors to Hanoi.

ranking.name: Bánh xèo
ranking.description: A rice batter with turmeric and coconut milk is fried in a hot pan into a large golden, crisp crepe, filled with shrimp, pork and bean sprouts, then wrapped in lettuce and dipped in fish sauce.
ranking.history: The "xèo" in "bánh xèo" is the sizzling sound made when the rice batter is poured into the hot pan, so the name directly describes the sound of cooking. This crepe is especially popular in central and southern Vietnam; the southern version is larger and often includes coconut milk, and shares common roots with similar Cambodian crepes. It is often made in the rainy season and at family gatherings, with everyone sitting together wrapping it in lettuce and dipping it in fish sauce to share.
